newsitem.title: USA: Kellogg Q2 U.S. cereal market share rises.
newsitem.headline: Kellogg Q2 U.S. cereal market share rises.

text.p: Kellogg Co, the leader of the $9.0 billion U.S. ready-to-eat cereal market, said Friday its domestic market share hit 33.8 percent in the second quarter, continuing a steady improvement over recent quarters.
Kellogg's market share stood at 33.2 percent in the first quarter, 32.9 percent in the fourth quarter of 1996, and 32.6 percent in the second and third quarters of 1996.

"We still think we are in an exciting business category," Joseph Stewart, senior vice president of corporate affairs, said of the U.S. cereal industry that was hurt by intense competition and price cuts a year ago.
He added that while the U.S. cereal industry overall is growing by about 1.4 percent on an annual basis, Kellogg expects it could grow at a two percent rate "over time."
This would be below the historic growth rate of two percent, but an improvement from a relatively flat 1996.

Stewart said Kellogg's North American cereal volume grew in the second quarter, but declined to give specifics. Growth was helped by its two newest cereals -- Honey Crunch Corn Flakes and Cocoa Frosted Flakes -- that hold an aggregate market share of between two and three percent.

Earlier, Kellogg reported second quarter results of $0.83 a share before a $0.04 charge, far above depressed-year ago results of $0.45 and beating the First Call consensus of $0.73. The results also beat some analysts' expectations that Kellogg would match the $0.77 a share results it posted in the 1995 quarter.
"Wonderful. Well-above expectations," said Goldman Sachs analyst Nomi Ghez, who had estimated Kellogg's second quarter at $0.75 a share.
"I have to believe that this shows that Kellogg is back on its feet," Ghez added.
Shares of Kellogg -- which also set a two-for-one-stock split and increased its quarterly dividend -- rose $4.25 to $96.125 a share on Friday morning.

Kellogg's year-ago earnings of $0.45 a share before an $0.08 charge reflected the impact of price cuts in the U.S. ready-to-eat cereal market. Kellogg responded by cutting costs and streamlining operations.
Sales in the second quarter rose four percent to $1.72 billion.
Stewart declined to say specifically if Kellogg expects the growth shown in the second quarter to be sustainable.
"We are confident in our long-term strategy and we're sticking to it long term," Stewart said.
He added that Kellogg's convenience foods, which posted annual sales of about $1.0 billion in 1996, grew at a double-digit percentage pace in the second quarter.
Kellogg also is investing to expand its international cereal business to capture business overseas.
